graders.evidence:
## What a Bloom filter is, and when it earns its place

A Bloom filter is a small, fixed-size structure that answers one question about a set: is this key in it? It is put in front of a slow lookup, such as a read from disk, so that the lookup only runs for keys that might be present.

The filter is an array of bits, all 0 to begin with, together with k hash functions. To add a key, the filter hashes it k times and sets the k bits that the hashes point to. To check a key, it hashes the key the same way and reads those k bits. If any of them is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set every one. If all of them are 1, the key probably was added.

The answer is only "probably" because different keys can set the same bits. A key that was never added can find all k of its bits already set by others, and the filter then reports a false positive. The reverse cannot happen. A bit that has been set is never cleared, so an added key always finds its bits set, and the filter never gives a false negative.

This asymmetry decides where the filter is useful. A "no" is certain, so the slow lookup can be skipped. A "yes" has to be confirmed by doing the lookup, and a false positive costs one lookup that found nothing. The filter pays off when many of the lookups ask for keys that are absent, or when a key could be in any of many places and the filter can rule most of them out.

The false positive rate depends on how full the array is. It rises as more keys set more bits. About 10 bits per key with 7 hash functions gives a rate near 1%. For a given array size and key count, the best number of hashes is the bits per key times ln 2, which is where 7 comes from at 10 bits per key. Computing 7 independent hashes per key would be costly, so implementations use double hashing: two real hash values produce all k bit positions.

LevelDB is a clear case. It stores its data in many files on disk and keeps one filter per file. A read checks each file's filter and skips every file whose filter says no, so the disk is read only for files that might hold the key.

The structure has limits that follow from how it works. It cannot remove a key, because clearing one of the key's bits could also erase another key that shares it. A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter, incrementing on add and decrementing on remove, and so allows removal. A filter also stores no keys and no values, so it cannot list what it contains or return the value for a key. It only says whether the real lookup is worth doing.

A Bloom filter is a small, fixed-size structure that answers whether a key is in a set. It is built to say "no" quickly, so that a slow lookup, such as a read from disk, can be skipped for keys that are not there.

To check a key, it hashes the key the same way and reads the same k bits. If any of them is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set every one. If all of them are 1, the key probably was added.

The "probably" comes from sharing. Each bit may have been set by a different key, so a key that was never added can find all of its k bits already set. That is a false positive, and the filter has no way to tell it apart from a real hit. A false negative cannot happen, since a bit that was set is never cleared. A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter, so that adding increments and removing decrements, at the cost of a larger array.

This shapes when a filter pays off. It helps when the lookup behind it is much slower than a few bit reads and many of the queries are for keys that are absent, since each of those ends at the filter instead of at the slow lookup. A present key always passes through the filter and still pays for the lookup, and a false positive costs one lookup that finds nothing. The filter also suits data that is added to and rarely deleted from, given that it cannot remove keys.

LevelDB is a good example. It keeps one filter per file on disk, so a read checks each file's filter and skips every file whose filter says no. Most files do not hold the key being read, and for those files the read costs a few bit checks in memory instead of a trip to disk.

## What a Bloom filter is, and when it pays off

A Bloom filter is a small, fixed-size structure that answers one question about a set of keys: has this key been added? It is built to answer that question quickly, so that a program can skip a slow lookup for a key that is not there.

The structure is an array of bits, all starting at 0, together with k hash functions. To add a key, the filter runs the key through each hash function and sets the k bits that the hashes point to. To check a key, it computes the same k positions and reads those bits. If any of them is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set every one. If all of them are 1, the key probably was added. Computing k positions does not require k independent hash functions. Double hashing derives all of them from two hash values, so the filter needs only two real hash functions.

The answer "probably" is where the filter can be wrong. Other keys set bits too, and the k bits for a key that was never added may all have been set by different keys that happened to share them. The filter then reports a key that is absent as present, which is a false positive. It never reports a key that was added as absent, so it gives no false negatives, and a "no" can always be trusted. As more keys are added the array fills with 1s and the false positive rate rises. With about 10 bits per key and 7 hash functions the rate is near 1%. For a given array size and number of keys, the best k is the bits per key times ln 2, which for 10 bits per key is about 7.

The filter cannot remove a key. Clearing one of a key's bits could also clear a bit that another key depends on, and that key would then read as absent, which would introduce false negatives. A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter, so that adding increments the counters and removing decrements them, at the cost of more space per position. The filter also cannot list the keys it holds or return a value for one. It only says yes, probably, or no, definitely.

Those properties decide when a filter is worth putting in front of a slow lookup. The filter helps in proportion to how many lookups it can turn away, and it can only turn away keys that are absent. If most lookups are for keys that exist, the filter says "probably" and the slow lookup runs anyway. If many lookups are for absent keys, each one the filter rejects costs a few bit reads in memory and no slow lookup, and the false positive rate sets how many absent keys still get through. The slow lookup also still has to be there for the keys that exist, since the filter returns no values.

LevelDB uses the filter this way. It keeps one filter per file on disk, and a read checks the filters before opening files. Every file whose filter says no is skipped, so the read goes to disk only for files that might hold the key.

Write the explainer section for a Go language guide, for a developer about to use defer to release resources. The question it answers: When does a deferred call run in Go, for someone using defer to release a resource?

Facts, each checked against the Go specification:

- `defer` schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, not at the end of the enclosing block.
- The arguments of the deferred call are evaluated when the `defer` statement runs, not when the call runs.
- For a method call, the receiver is evaluated when the `defer` statement runs too.
- Deferred calls run last in, first out.
- Deferred calls also run when the function panics.
- A deferred function literal can read and set the function's named results.
- In a loop each iteration adds a deferred call, and none run until the function returns, so `defer f.Close()` in a loop keeps every file open until then.
- A deferred call of a nil function value panics when the call runs, not at the `defer` statement.
- Since Go 1.14 the compiler inlines most defers at function exit, so a defer costs a few nanoseconds.

## When a deferred call runs

A `defer` statement schedules a function call to run when the surrounding function returns. It is the usual way to pair acquiring a resource with releasing it: the `Close` is written on the line after the `Open`, and it runs however the function ends.

The call waits for the function, not for the block it was written in. A `defer` inside an `if` or a `for` body runs when the whole function returns, after the block has long finished. It also runs if the function panics, so the resource is released while the panic unwinds. When a function defers several calls, they run last in, first out, so a resource opened later is released before one opened earlier.

The `defer` statement itself runs at its place in the function, and that is when the function value and its arguments are evaluated. Only the call is postponed. In this example the deferred call prints 1, because `n` had that value when the statement ran:

```go
n := 1
defer fmt.Println(n)
n = 2
```

A method call is treated the same way, and its receiver is evaluated when the statement runs. After `defer f.Close()`, assigning a different file to `f` does not change which file is closed.

A loop adds one deferred call per iteration, and none of them run until the function returns. With `defer f.Close()` in a loop over file names, every file stays open until then. To release each file at the end of its iteration, move the loop body into a function of its own, so that each call returns, and runs its deferred calls, once per file.

A deferred function literal can read and set the function's named results, which lets it report a failure that happens during cleanup:

```go
func write(name string, data []byte) (err error) {
	f, err := os.Create(name)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer func() {
		if cerr := f.Close(); err == nil {
			err = cerr
		}
	}()
	_, err = f.Write(data)
	return err
}
```

If the deferred expression is a nil function value, the `defer` statement succeeds and the panic happens later, when the call runs at function exit.

Since Go 1.14 the compiler inlines most defers at the function's exit, so a `defer` costs a few nanoseconds.

cases.promptMarkdown:
Write the explainer section for the groupcache README, for a developer deciding whether to use groupcache. The question it answers: How does groupcache work, for someone deciding whether to use it?

Facts, each checked against the code:

- groupcache is a Go library for caching across a cluster of processes.
- Every process holds part of the cache and serves it to the others, so there are no cache servers.
- Peers are given to a process through `SetPeers()`.
- Keys sit on a consistent hash ring. A process finds a key's owner by hashing against its own copy of the ring, with no network call.
- Each key has one owner.
- `Get()` checks the main cache (keys the process owns) and the hot cache (copies of keys peers own) first, then asks the owner.
- The owner runs the `Getter` and passes the value back through a `Sink`.
- The hot cache is bounded relative to the main cache, so copies of peer-owned keys cannot take over the keys the process owns.
- When a peer joins or leaves, only the keys on its part of the ring change owner.
- Singleflight allows one in-flight load per key. A million `Get("FOO")` calls run the `Getter` once.
- If the owner is unreachable, the asking process runs the `Getter` itself, so the `Getter` can run on more than one process.
- `Set()`, `Remove()` and `RemoveKeys()` go to the owner and then to every other peer, best effort, so values should carry an expiry.
- The default cache is an LRU. The Otter cache uses lock-free S3-FIFO eviction.
- HTTP is the default transport.
- Stats are OpenTelemetry metrics.
- There is no global state.

## How groupcache works

groupcache is a Go library for caching across a cluster of processes. Each process holds part of the cache and serves it to the others, so the cluster has no cache servers to run. A process learns who its peers are through `SetPeers()`.

Keys are placed on a consistent hash ring, and every key has one owner. A process finds the owner of a key by hashing it against its own copy of the ring. When a peer joins or leaves, the keys on its part of the ring change owner and the rest of the ring is untouched.

A `Get()` looks in two local caches first. The main cache holds the keys the process owns, and the hot cache holds copies of keys that peers own. The hot cache is bounded relative to the main cache, so copies of peer-owned keys cannot take over the space for the keys the process owns. If neither cache has the key, the process asks the owner. The owner runs the `Getter`, the function you supply to load a value, and passes the result back through a `Sink`.

`Set()`, `Remove()` and `RemoveKeys()` go to the owner and then to every other peer. Delivery is best effort, so a peer can miss an update and keep serving the old value. Values should therefore carry an expiry.

The default cache is an LRU. The Otter cache is an alternative that uses lock-free S3-FIFO eviction. HTTP is the default transport between peers, stats are reported as OpenTelemetry metrics, and the library keeps no global state.

cases.name: writing-prose-write-ahead-log
cases.promptMarkdown:
Write the explainer section for a database internals guide, for a developer who has not seen how databases survive a crash. The question it answers: How does a write-ahead log keep a database from losing committed data in a crash?

Facts, each checked against the Postgres documentation:

- A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change.
- The database changes data pages in memory and writes them to disk later.
- Before it changes a page, it appends a record describing the change to the log.
- A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync. The data pages do not have to be.
- Appending to the end of a file is sequential, so flushing the log costs much less than flushing pages scattered across the data files.
- After a crash the database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page.
- Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it, so replay skips records a page already has.
- A checkpoint writes all modified pages to disk and notes the log position. The log before it can be deleted or reused.
- Postgres calls this the WAL, and replicas stay current by replaying the same records.
- Postgres stores the log in 16 MB segment files by default.
- In Postgres an LSN is a byte position in the log.

graders.evidence:
## How a write-ahead log survives a crash

A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change. It exists so that a crash cannot take away a transaction the database has already reported as committed.

The risk comes from how the database handles data. It changes data pages in memory and writes them to disk later, so a power failure in between destroys changes that exist only in memory. Writing every changed page to disk at commit would close that gap, but the pages live at scattered places across the data files, and each commit would wait on many separate writes.

The log removes that cost. Before the database changes a page, it appends a record describing the change to the log. A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync, and the data pages do not have to be. Appending to the end of a file is sequential, so flushing the log costs much less than flushing pages scattered across the data files. When a commit returns, the transaction's changes are on disk as log records, whether or not any data page has been written.

After a crash, the database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page, which rebuilds the changes that were lost from memory. Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it. Some pages reached disk before the crash, so replay compares the two numbers and skips any record that the page already has. In Postgres, which calls this log the WAL, an LSN is a byte position in the log.

Replay starts at a checkpoint to keep it short. A checkpoint writes all modified pages to disk and notes the log position. Every record before that position describes a change already on disk, so that part of the log can be deleted or reused.
